name: Death of Henry V of England
summary: Henry V of England, aged 36 and at the peak of his power as heir to France under the Treaty of Troyes (1420), dies of dysentery at Vincennes on August 31, 1422. He leaves a nine-month-old son, Henry VI, as heir to both the English crown and (under Troyes) the French one. Charles VI of France dies weeks later; Henry VI theoretically becomes king of both realms. But the minority government proves unable to consolidate the conquest; Charles VII (the 'Dauphin' Henry V had declared illegitimate) rallies French resistance, and Joan of Arc's campaigns beginning 1429 reverse the English position.

_quarry.structural_significance: Henry V's premature death unravels the most ambitious English territorial conquest; the weakness of a minority government (Henry VI's regency) is ultimately fatal to the dual monarchy project; the French national resurgence catalyzed by Joan of Arc is only possible because of the power vacuum created by Henry V's death; his son Henry VI's mental illness eventually triggers the Wars of the Roses
